findings.issue: Source 'he had converse with the nymph' is a euphemism; candidate 'he slept with the nymph' is slightly more explicit but a sensible reading. Same softness shift in p13 ('would have had converse with me' -> 'wanted to lie with me').
Source 'the most surpassing comeliness and beauty'; candidate 'the most surpassing handsomeness and beauty' is clumsy and the word 'handsomeness' reads awkwardly.
findings.fix: The son of Hippolochus answered, “Son of Tydeus, why do you ask about my family line? Men come and go like the leaves on the trees from year to year. The wind scatters the autumn leaves on the ground, but when spring returns the forest bursts into bud with fresh vines. It is the same with the generations of mankind: the new spring up as the old pass away. But if you want to know my descent, many people know it well. There is a city in the heart of Argos, pasture land of horses, called Ephyra. Sisyphus lived there, the craftiest of all mankind. He was the son of Aeolus, and he had a son named Glaucus, who was the father of Bellerophon. Heaven gave Bellerophon the most surpassing good looks and beauty. But Proetus plotted his ruin. Proetus was the stronger, and he drove Bellerophon out of the land of the Argives, over which Zeus had made Proetus ruler. The reason was that Antea, the wife of Proetus, lusted after Bellerophon and wanted him to lie with her in secret. Bellerophon was an honorable man and refused, so she told lies about him to Proetus. ‘Proetus,’ she said, ‘kill Bellerophon or die yourself, for he wanted to lie with me against my will.’ The king was angry, but he shrank from killing Bellerophon. Instead he sent him to Lycia with lying letters of introduction, written on a folded tablet and full of ill against the man who carried it. He told Bellerophon to show these letters to his father-in-law, so that he would die that way. Bellerophon went to Lycia, and the gods escorted him safely.

findings.issue: Source 'when he sailed the seas upon that voyage during which he carried off Helen'; candidate 'on the voyage that carried off Helen' makes the voyage the agent and loses that Paris himself carried Helen off.
findings.fix: His mother went into the house and called her waiting-women, and they gathered the matrons from all over the city. Then she went down to her fragrant storeroom, where her embroidered robes were kept. These were the work of Sidonian women, whom Paris had brought over from Sidon when he sailed the seas on the voyage during which he carried off Helen. Hecuba took out the largest robe, the one most beautifully rich with embroidery, to give to Athena. It glittered like a star and lay at the very bottom of the chest. She set off with it, and many matrons went with her.

findings.issue: Source 'the fair house of Alexandrus, which he had built for him by the foremost builders... They had built him his house, storehouse, and courtyard'; candidate 'built it for him, with a house, storehouse, and courtyard' is circular (a house built with a house) and blurs that the builders made the house, storehouse and courtyard.
findings.fix: While they were praying to the daughter of great Zeus, Hector went to the fine house of Paris. The foremost builders in the land had built it for him: a house, storehouse, and courtyard near those of Priam and Hector on the acropolis. Hector went in, holding a spear eleven cubits long. Its bronze point gleamed ahead of him, fastened to the shaft by a ring of gold. He found Paris inside the house, busy with his armor, his shield and cuirass, and handling his curved bow. Argive Helen sat there too with her women, giving them their various tasks. When Hector saw Paris, he rebuked him with words of scorn. “Sir,” he said, “you do wrong to nurse this bitterness. The people are dying as they fight around this town of ours. You would blame anyone else you saw shirking his part in the fight. Up, then, or before long the city will be in flames.”
